justification: The passage states the wear pattern directly: "Wear is not spread evenly along the chain either. It gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel" — exactly the two locations named in B. A is contradicted by "a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter is usually condemned on a single bad metre," which is the opposite of every link losing a fifth. Salt corrosion (C) is never mentioned, and the inshore/narrow-water detail (D) belongs to Cadell's concession about scope, not to where wear gathers.

The scope passage explains the offset as normal swinging, not failure: "wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart." That is C. B reverses the stated relation (more chain, not less, means a wider circle); A generalises the single 31-metres-for-11-metres instance into a rule the text never states; and D is unsupported — the text says the district "lifts each of them once every three years" with no early-lift trigger for wander.

The lightship paragraph exists to make the point that uncertainty of position predates Prigent's loggers: her logs "carry, watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks, because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it," and Fewtrell closes with "'We knew the shoal was under us... Where we were over it was another question.'" That is A. B is contradicted by "does not sit still either"; C misreads the withdrawal, which the text attributes to the harbour board setting "the cost of her crew against a lamp on a hull that needed none," not to a post-war trend; D turns a shared uncertainty into a comparison of vigilance the text never draws.

The text ends the Cadell/Prigent exchange with a partial retreat: "Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved." That is D verbatim in substance. A overstates it into a full surrender that the same sentence denies; C invents a chronology (the two aids lost "in ten years, both in the same storm" are offered as too thin a series, not as the origin of his practice); and B substitutes a cost argument for the one he actually makes, which is that "a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails."

The piece walks through the mechanics of holding a floating light on station — "A floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored, and a mooring has to be slack" — and then sets Cadell against Prigent over how much slack, closing unresolved: "Neither record disposes of the other... Prigent would like another ten years of loggers. Cadell would like a February." That is B. A and D take single paragraphs (the lightship, her crew's cost) for the whole, and C advocates a position the text explicitly declines to settle.

The passage states directly that wear 'gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel', which is exactly B. A is contradicted by the opening of that same sentence, 'Wear is not spread evenly along the chain either', and by 'a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter is usually condemned on a single bad metre' — the fifth-of-diameter loss is a local condemnation threshold, not a state every link reaches in three years. C introduces salt corrosion, which the text never mentions at all, and D borrows 'where the water is narrow' from the later Cadell concession about inshore aids, where it describes his change of position on scope, not any distribution of wear.

The scope paragraph explains that 'wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart', so an off-chart buoy is presumptively riding its normal swinging circle rather than having shifted its sinker — C. B reverses the stated relation (more chain, not less, means a wider circle). A over-reads the single instance of 'thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water' into a rule, when the whole article turns on the fact that masters choose different scopes and Cadell 'lays his buoys long'. D is unsupported: the only lifting schedule given is that the district 'lifts each of them once every three years', with no provision for an early lift on account of wander.

The lightship paragraph exists to make the point that positional uncertainty is old news: her logs 'carry, watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks, because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it', capped by Fewtrell's 'We knew the shoal was under us... Where we were over it was another question' — uncertainty long predating Prigent, who has only been 'fitting position loggers inside the hulls since 2019'. That same 'does not sit still either' kills B, which claims the vessel held station better than a buoy. C seizes on the one clause about the harbour board setting 'the cost of her crew against a lamp on a hull that needed none', but that explains one withdrawal in 1968, not a coast-wide end of manned stations 'after the war', and it is not what the paragraph is built around. D invents a comparison of vigilance with today's crews that the text never makes.

The text ends the dispute paragraph with 'Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved' — precisely D. That sentence also refutes A, since a partial concession with the outer stations held is not giving the practice up. B attributes a cost argument to him that he never makes; his stated ground is survival — 'a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails' — with no comparison of replacement prices anywhere in the piece. C misuses the storm, which is offered only as evidence 'too thin a series to show whether a long mooring saves buoys or has merely been lucky', and cannot be the origin of a practice held by a master who 'has had the Marram for thirty-one years'.

The piece runs the buoy 43 lift and the mechanics of scope — 'A floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored, and a mooring has to be slack' — straight into the Cadell/Prigent disagreement about how much slack, which it explicitly leaves open: 'Neither record disposes of the other... Prigent would like another ten years of loggers. Cadell would like a February.' That is B. A takes the single lightship paragraph for the whole. C makes the writer an advocate for loggers, but the wish for more of them is reported as Prigent's, and the closing line has buoy 43 going back 'on the scope its master chose'. D is built from one clause about the harbour board's crew costs; nothing in the text tracks a rising cost of maintaining marks.

The passage names the consequence outright: "Om en glipa fick sitta kvar obemärkt drog luften in, och det som skulle ha blivit kol brann i stället upp; ett par timmar räckte för att göra en hel veckas arbete till aska." B restates that exact chain — air enters, the wood burns up instead of charring, and the burn is lost. A and C invert the mechanism (slow cooling / a charring that merely drags on) against "Veden skulle förkolna, inte brinna", and D hardens it into an absolute, "ofelbart ... oavsett hur snabbt kolaren hinner ingripa", which the text's conditional "fick sitta kvar obemärkt" and the whole rationale for the kolare's round-the-clock watch contradict.

The third paragraph gives both halves of the contrast: "Träkol är sprött. Varje omlastning och varje mil på ojämna vägar bröt ner bitarna till finkol och damm", while "Tjäran låg stilla i sina tunnor och kunde fraktas nedför älven, lastas om och lagras över en vinter utan att förlora i värde", concluding "Tjärtunnor gick att föra långa vägar på vatten, medan kolet i praktiken måste fram till hyttan över frusen mark, på slädar och helst utan en enda omlastning." D is that statement. A reverses which product was fragile; B's bulk-and-value-per-barrel argument is never made in the text; C's claim that resin-rich pine grew only far from the hyttor is unsupported — the text ties tar wood to barked stumps and roots, not to distance.

Nyfeldt's objection is stated in full: "Vresfallets bruk ägde eller disponerade skog i en ring kring hyttan, och utanför den ringen hade bruket varken avverkningsrätt eller skäl att köpa. Det Bostrand tar för en transportgräns skulle då vara en ägogräns, och kartan skulle visa vem som ägde marken snarare än hur långt en slädlast nådde." A is that ownership-boundary reading. B inverts the causal direction she proposes; C attributes to her a blanket epistemic claim about kolräkenskaper that she never makes; D borrows the surname-only föreståndare from Bostrand's own note on the material's unevenness, which is not part of her critique.

The overlap in suppliers — "av dem som sålde kol till Vresfallet levererade ungefär en tredjedel också tjära något år" — is made workable by the seasonal split the text marks explicitly: "Årstiderna skilde dem åt. Tjärdalarna brändes helst på försommaren ... medan kolmilorna restes från sensommaren och in i oktober", which is C. A is contradicted by "Kolarens skicklighet satt i vakthållningen; tjärbrännarens satt i själva klyvningen och resningen" — the two crafts rest on different skills. B overshoots "ungefär en tredjedel" into nearly every household, and D's coercion by rising kärl fees is nowhere in the text, which mentions the fee only as a deduction from the kol price.

The passage states the outcome explicitly: "Om en glipa fick sitta kvar obemärkt drog luften in, och det som skulle ha blivit kol brann i stället upp; ett par timmar räckte för att göra en hel veckas arbete till aska." B restates exactly that chain (air in, wood burns instead of charring, the charring is lost). A contradicts it by having the mila cool and the wood remain half-charred; C invents a prolonged process beyond "sex till nio dygn" that the text never claims; D is an absolutization ("ofelbart", "oavsett hur snabbt") contradicted by the conditional "fick sitta kvar obemärkt" and by the point of the round-the-clock watch.

The stated mechanism is fragility versus durability in transport: "Träkol är sprött. Varje omlastning och varje mil på ojämna vägar bröt ner bitarna till finkol och damm", while "Tjäran låg stilla i sina tunnor och kunde fraktas nedför älven, lastas om och lagras över en vinter utan att förlora i värde", and "Den skillnaden avgjorde var hantverken kunde bedrivas." D matches this. A is the exact reversal of which product was fragile; B substitutes bulk and value per barrel, which the passage never gives as the reason; C claims the resinous pine grew only far from the hyttor, which is not addressed.

Nyfeldt's objection is that the boundary may be a property line: "Vresfallets bruk ägde eller disponerade skog i en ring kring hyttan, och utanför den ringen hade bruket varken avverkningsrätt eller skäl att köpa. Det Bostrand tar för en transportgräns skulle då vara en ägogräns". A states precisely this. B inverts the causation (the bruk buying forest out to the sledge limit); C is a blanket epistemic claim she never makes; D concerns the 1870s foreman writing only surnames, which is Bostrand's own note on uneven material, not Nyfeldt's objection.

The passage supplies the seasonal complementarity that makes the combination workable: "Årstiderna skilde dem åt. Tjärdalarna brändes helst på försommaren ... medan kolmilorna restes från sensommaren och in i oktober", alongside "av dem som sålde kol till Vresfallet levererade ungefär en tredjedel också tjära något år." C follows. A is contradicted by "Tjärbränningen krävde annat virke och annat kunnande" and by the split between vakthållning and klyvning/resning; B overstates "ungefär en tredjedel" into nearly every household; D invents coercion via the kärl fee, which appears only in the pay arithmetic.
